description.en: Awaiting tasks one by one wastes time when they could overlap. asyncio.gather runs coroutines concurrently and collects their results in order — the core of fast async I/O.

story_variants.en:
## Stop Waiting in Line

"Three network calls, two seconds each," Vaathiyaar says. "Await them one after another and you wait six seconds. But they don't depend on each other — so **run them concurrently** and you wait about *two*. That's what **`asyncio.gather`** does: launch several coroutines at once, then collect their results together, in the order you passed them."

### gather in One Line

```
results = await asyncio.gather(task1(), task2(), task3())
```

Each `taskN()` is a coroutine. `gather` schedules them all on the event loop so their `await` points overlap (while one waits on I/O, another runs), then returns a list of results **in argument order** — not completion order. That ordering guarantee is what makes it safe to `results[0]`, `results[1]`, and so on.

```
async def double(n):
    return n * 2

await asyncio.gather(double(1), double(2), double(3))  ->  [2, 4, 6]
```

> **Vaathiyaar's rule:** whenever independent awaitables pile up — API calls, DB queries, file reads — gather them. Sequential `await` in a loop is the #1 cause of slow async code.

Today you implement `run_all(nums)` — concurrently double each number with `asyncio.gather` and return the results list.

instruction.en: Complete `run_all(nums)` so it concurrently doubles each number using `asyncio.gather` and returns the list of results in input order. q.en: Why does asyncio.gather make independent I/O tasks finish sooner?
q.ta: சார்பற்ற I/O பணிகளை asyncio.gather ஏன் விரைவாக முடிக்கச் செய்கிறது?

en: It skips the await points inside the coroutines
It makes every single coroutine execute faster
It runs each coroutine on a separate CPU core
Their await points overlap: while one waits, another runs

uth_example:
import asyncio

async def fetch_price(item, delay):
    await asyncio.sleep(delay)
    return {"item": item, "price": len(item) * 10}

async def main():
    orders = [("tea", 0.03), ("coffee", 0.01), ("juice", 0.02)]
    coros = [fetch_price(name, d) for name, d in orders]
    results = await asyncio.gather(*coros)     # all run at once
    total = sum(r["price"] for r in results)
    return results, total

results, total = asyncio.run(main())
print([r["item"] for r in results], "total:", total)

under_the_hood.summary: When three tasks under gather each send a request and await the reply, the loop registers all three sockets with the OS selector in one wait; replies are handled as they arrive, so total time is close to the slowest call rather than the sum.

steps.title: All requests leave before any reply
steps.body: With `gather(get('A'), get('B'), get('C'))`, task A sends its request and awaits the reply. That await hands control back, so the loop runs task B, which sends its request and awaits, then task C. Within a few milliseconds all three requests are in flight.

steps.title: One OS call watches every socket
steps.body: The loop now has nothing ready to run, so it calls the selector (epoll on Linux) once with all three sockets. The operating system puts the thread to sleep until any socket has data. No CPU is used while waiting, and adding a fourth request adds no extra waiting thread.

steps.title: Replies wake tasks in arrival order
steps.body: If B's reply arrives at 1.2 s, the selector returns B's socket; the loop schedules task B, which reads the data and finishes. A's reply arrives at 1.9 s and C's at 2.0 s. gather completes when the last one does.

props.caption: Finishing order is set by the network, not the code

steps.title: Time is the maximum, not the sum
steps.body: Sequentially, 1.9 + 1.2 + 2.0 = 5.1 seconds. Concurrently, the waits overlap and the total is about 2.0 seconds, the slowest call. The more calls you overlap, the bigger the gain, until the server or your connection limit becomes the bottleneck.

steps.title: Results keep the call order
steps.body: Although B finished first, `results` is `[A_result, B_result, C_result]`, matching the order of the arguments, so you can unpack them directly: `a, b, c = await asyncio.gather(...)`.

under_the_hood.takeaway: gather gets its speed from overlapping waits: every request is sent first, then one OS wait covers them all. Total time tracks the slowest call, which is why independent I/O should never be awaited one by one.
